# Part 4: Governance by Design

## 4.1 The governance operating model

Governance that arrives after the architecture is a review, not a control: it can find defects, withhold approval and write findings, but by the time it looks the decisions that determined the risk have been made, coded, deployed and depended upon. Everything a late reviewer can do costs more than what an early designer could have done for free.

**Governance by design** means one thing, operational rather than aspirational: every architectural decision has a governance consequence, decided at the same moment as the architectural decision, by a named person, leaving an artifact. Four elements, all required: without simultaneity you get retrofit, without a named person a committee that has not decided, without an artifact a claim rather than a control, without coupling to an architectural decision a policy library nobody reads.

The test is not whether an organization has a policy but whether you can pick any architectural decision at random from a live system, ask who decided its governance consequence and on what date, and get an artifact rather than a team name. An architecture review board applies the same standard: a team that can explain every control but attach no signed artifact has its paper deferred rather than rejected, and since boards sit monthly or quarterly that missing attachment costs more elapsed time than producing it would.

```
 DESIGN MOMENT                    GOVERNANCE MOMENT
 -------------                    -----------------
 [Architectural decision] ------> [Governance decision]
          |                                |
          |                                v
          |                       [Named owner records it]
          |                                |
          v                                v
 [Running system]   <-----------   [Artifact emitted]
          |                                |
          |                                v
          |                       [Evidence register row]
          |                                |
          +----- operating evidence ------>+
                (the artifact regenerates
                 on a trigger, not on request)
```

### Three lines of defense and where the model breaks for AI

The **three lines of defense** model assigns risk ownership to the first line, which builds and operates; oversight and challenge to the second, which sets policy and monitors; and independent assurance to the third, internal audit, reporting to the board rather than to management. It is the default in every regulated enterprise and the right starting point for AI, and it breaks in four specific ways: knowing which four separates an operating model from an org chart.

| Break | Mechanism | Architectural consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Competence inversion** | The second line cannot challenge what it does not understand. In most enterprises the only people who understand the retrieval design work in the first line | Second line must hold an independent technical capability or its challenge is procedural only. Budget for it or admit the gap |
| **Speed asymmetry** | First line ships prompt changes in hours. Second line reviews on a monthly cadence. The reviewed artifact is not the deployed artifact | Prompt assets and tool definitions must be version-controlled and change-gated in the same pipeline as code, or oversight reviews history |
| **Vendor opacity** | The model is a third party's artifact. First line cannot inspect it, second line cannot test it and third line cannot audit it | Assurance shifts from inspection to contract, configuration evidence and behavioral evaluation. The evaluation suite becomes the audit evidence |
| **Diffuse first line** | With assistants deployed enterprise-wide, the first line is every employee, not a product team | Governance attaches to the platform and the entry point rather than to the use case, because there is no use-case owner to attach it to |

⧉ **The competence inversion is the single biggest structural risk in the operating model.** A second line reviewing AI systems with a questionnaire whose answers it cannot evaluate produces the appearance of independent challenge without the substance, durably, because the artifact trail looks complete. The remedy is not more questions but one or two people in the second line who can read a design, reproduce an evaluation result and demand a replay as of right.

Sequencing compounds the structural failures: controls designed inside the first line get redesigned when the second line first sees them, after commitments to the business have been made. Second-line review and challenge belong before build starts, not before go-live.

### The AI governance committee

**Decision rule for a committee: if it cannot say no on a Tuesday and have that stick, it is a forum, not a committee.**

A working charter has seven elements and no more: purpose, the decisions reserved to the committee; scope, what is in and out; membership by role rather than name, with quorum; the decision rights it holds exclusively; escalation routes up and down; cadence, including an out-of-cycle path; and a review clause for the charter itself.

Membership that functions: a chair who is an executive with profit-and-loss or enterprise accountability, not a technologist; the second-line risk owner; legal, meaning whoever can bind the organization's view of privilege and confidentiality in a professional-services or in-house context; privacy, usually not that same person; security; the delivery function head whose systems are governed; and one business representative from the most affected function. Internal audit observes and does not vote, because voting destroys its independence.

What the committee must not do, in four prohibitions:

1. **It must not design.** A committee that redesigns the retrieval pipeline has taken first-line accountability and destroyed its ability to challenge the result.
2. **It must not become the approval path for every deployment.** A committee approving low-tier and moderate-tier systems is a bottleneck that will be routed around, invisibly.
3. **It must not own controls.** Owning a control means operating it, and a committee cannot operate anything because it cannot be paged.
4. **It must not resolve disputes by consensus into vagueness.** The output of a contested item is a decision with a dissent recorded, not a softened sentence.

### Policy, standard, procedure and control

These four words are used interchangeably in most organizations and the confusion is expensive: an auditor tests them differently and a court reads them differently.

| Artifact | Answers | Binding on | Changes | Approved by | Failure mode when confused |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Policy** | What we will and will not do, and why | Everyone in scope | Rarely, at board or executive level | Board or executive committee | Policies written at procedure granularity become obsolete in a quarter and expose the organization to a documented gap between stated and actual practice |
| **Standard** | What good looks like, in measurable terms | Every system in a class | Annually or on material change | AI governance committee or function head | Standards written as aspirations cannot be tested, so compliance cannot be asserted |
| **Procedure** | How a named role does a named task, in order | The role performing it | Freely, by the owner | Process owner | Procedures elevated to policy freeze the operating model and require board action to fix a form field |
| **Control** | The specific mechanism that prevents, detects or corrects, plus its failure behavior | The system or the operator | On design change | Control owner, ratified by second line | A control described without its failure behavior is an assumption, per the guardrail doctrine in 4.4 |

The chain is one-directional: policy commitments decompose into standards, standards into procedures, procedures into the controls that enforce or evidence them. A control that cannot be traced upward to a policy commitment is either unnecessary or reveals an unwritten policy, and both findings are useful.

#### Detecting regulatory change

A material change in the regulatory character of a use is one of the nine re-tier triggers in 4.2 and the only one no system emits. A tool added to an allowlist, a corpus change, a model version change and an incident announce themselves from inside the estate; a regulatory change happens outside it, on someone else's timetable, and reaches the organization only if someone is looking. **A trigger with no detection mechanism and no named owner is a sentence in a policy, not a control.**

A single-jurisdiction organization absorbs this in counsel's ordinary reading. In a multi-jurisdiction estate it is a standing loop with a cadence, an owner and an output, and the characteristic failure is treating it as a project that produces a register once: one current eighteen months ago is worse than none, because it will be relied on.

Three inputs work, in ascending order of cost:

1. **A monitored source list per jurisdiction, each source with a named reader and a cadence.** Regulator publications, supervisory statements, enforcement actions and legislative trackers, for every jurisdiction where the organization operates, its users sit or its data rests. The discipline is the named reader, not the list: a source list monitored by a function is monitored by nobody.
2. **The trade and sector bodies.** They see consultations and drafts before anything is final, converting a future compliance deadline into a present design constraint early enough to be cheap: the input most under-used by organizations that already pay the membership.
3. **Counsel's standing instruction to flag.** Counsel, internal and external, meet change in the course of unrelated work. The instruction must be standing and specific: flag anything bearing on these use classes, in these jurisdictions, for these data classes, to this named person, on sight. Counsel asked at renewal will report at renewal.

The step most organizations miss comes after detection: the change is understood, then nobody can say which live systems it reaches, so the response is either an estate-wide review nobody funds or a silence that later reads as a decision. **Maintaining the mapping from a regulatory change to the population of live systems it touches is the actual work.** Not a document: a query against the system inventory filtered on recorded purpose, affected population, jurisdiction and data class, which is why those four fields are mandatory on the system record rather than optional metadata. An inventory that cannot say which live systems process special-category data about individuals in a named jurisdiction for a named purpose is an asset list, not a governance instrument.

The query is followed by a re-evidencing schedule: for each system returned, what must be re-assessed, by whom and by when, with an owner and a date rather than an intention. ⚠ Whether a change alters the obligations attaching to a use stays with counsel. The architectural obligation is narrower and discharged in-house: produce the affected population in days rather than quarters, and show the question was asked on the date it arose.

### Where governance sits

Four placements, each with a real trade-off and no correct answer independent of the organization's risk profile and the credibility of available functions.

| Placement | Works when | Fails because |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Under legal or the General Counsel** | Regulatory and privilege exposure dominates; the function needs standing to say no; the organization is a professional-services firm or heavily regulated | Engineering treats it as external, so decisions arrive late; legal rarely carries the technical depth to challenge design; risk of governing the paperwork rather than the system |
| **Under risk or compliance** | A mature second line already exists with model risk experience | AI arrives faster than second-line cadence; the model risk lineage biases toward statistical validation techniques that do not transfer to language systems |
| **Under technology or the Chief Information Officer** | Speed and technical fluency dominate; the organization is pre-regulatory | Independence is gone. Technology governing technology is first-line self-assessment wearing a second-line label |
| **A standalone AI governance function reporting to the executive** | Volume justifies dedicated headcount; the organization has multiple regulated jurisdictions | Expensive, slow to establish credibility and creates a fourth party that the existing three lines route around unless decision rights are taken from them explicitly |

**Decision rule for placement: put governance where the authority to stop a deployment already exists, then buy the technical competence it lacks. Do not put it where the competence exists and hope authority follows.**

In a governance, risk management and compliance consultancy led by a General Counsel, the first placement is usually correct and its named weakness decisive: the function must acquire or contract the ability to read a design and reproduce an evaluation, or challenge stays procedural.

## 4.2 Risk tiering

Tiering is the highest-leverage governance mechanism, because it is the only one deciding how much of everything else applies. The classification sets the control budget, rather than the control set defining the risk. Get it wrong high and the organization builds a control regime it cannot staff, which collapses into exception granting. Get it wrong low and the controls that would have caught the problem were never required.

Two questions come before any scoring: who classifies the use case, and against what stated tolerance for residual risk the resulting control set is judged. Classify early, for a calendar reason as much as a governance one: an unclassified use case waits for a committee date, and that delay routinely exceeds the engineering effort in dispute.

The first question is answered under self-tiering below. The second has a short answer most organizations never write down. **The tolerance is a written statement, per tier, of the residual risk the organization is prepared to carry**, set by the AI governance committee under its charter, reviewed annually and recorded on the tier record next to the scores. Without it, "adequate controls" means whatever the person saying it needs it to mean, and the adequacy judgment migrates to whoever is under the most delivery pressure. With it the test is mechanical: a control set leaving residual risk above the stated tolerance for its tier is redesigned until it does not, or escalated for explicit acceptance under the non-delegable rule in 4.7. There is no third route, and in particular no route in which the risk is recorded and the system goes live on the strength of having recorded it.

### The eight input dimensions

| Dimension | Question | 0 | 4 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Autonomy** | How much happens without a human in the path | Draft only, human issues | Multi-step agent executing state-changing tools to completion |
| **Reversibility** | Can the effect be undone, by whom and at what cost | Fully reversible by the operator in seconds | Irreversible, or reversible only through legal process |
| **Stakes** | What is the magnitude of a single bad outcome | Trivial rework | Material financial, safety, legal or reputational loss |
| **Affected population** | Who bears the consequence and did they choose to | One internal user who chose the tool | External individuals, at scale, without practical opt-out |
| **Data sensitivity** | What classes of data enter the system | Public or synthetic | Special-category personal data, privileged material or regulated records |
| **External exposure** | Who can reach it and what can reach it | Internal only, closed corpus | Public interface, or ingests untrusted third-party content |
| **Regulatory character** | Does a regime attach specific obligations to this use | None identified | Named regime with specific obligations for this use class ⚠ |
| **Novelty** | Has the organization operated this shape before | Third or later deployment of a proven pattern | First of kind for the organization or the vendor |

Score each 0 to 4. Sum runs 0 to 32. Novelty decays: a first-of-kind scores 4 at launch and steps down as operating evidence accumulates, which is a feature rather than a fudge, because the risk it represents is genuinely the absence of evidence.

### Scoring, tiers and the four overrides

```
 INPUTS (8)                 SCORE          TIER        AUTHORITY
 ----------                 -----          ----        ---------
 autonomy         \
 reversibility     \
 stakes             \
 affected pop       >--> additive sum --> T4 crit --> board / exec
 data sensitivity  /     0 to 32          T3 high --> committee
 external exposure/      then four        T2 mod  --> function head
 regulatory char /       overrides        T1 low  --> named owner
 novelty        /
                              ^
                              |
   OVERRIDE 1  any single dimension at 4 floors the tier at T3
   OVERRIDE 2  output affects legal rights, entitlements,
               employment, credit, health or liberty: floor T3
               and require human decision authority
   OVERRIDE 3  autonomy >= 3 AND reversibility <= 1: floor T4
   OVERRIDE 4  novelty = 4: one tier above computed, capped at
               T4, for the first operating period, then re-score
```

Band boundaries: T1 is 0 to 8, T2 is 9 to 16, T3 is 17 to 24, T4 is 25 to 32, before overrides. The overrides matter more than the arithmetic. A pure additive score lets eight moderate answers outvote one catastrophic one, which is exactly backwards for risk. The overrides restore the asymmetry.

### What changes per tier

| Dimension | T1 Low | T2 Moderate | T3 High | T4 Critical |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Approval** | Named owner self-certifies against the standard | Function head | AI governance committee | Executive or board, on committee recommendation |
| **Oversight placement** | None required; sampled review optional | Review after action, sampled at a defined rate | Human in the middle, or approval before action on the consequential branch | Approval before action, with a second reviewer on irreversible steps |
| **Eval rigor** | Smoke set, run at change | Eval set per architecture, regression suite, run at change | Above, plus labeled retrieval set on schedule, segmentation by affected group, adversarial set | Above, plus independent evaluation by a party that did not build it, plus pre-deployment red team |
| **Logging depth** | Request metadata, model identifier, outcome | Above, plus full input and output, trace identifier, per-request identity | Above, plus retrieval provenance, tool calls with arguments, suppressed and refused actions, reviewer identity and decision | Above, plus immutable write-once storage, independent time source and log integrity verification |
| **Review cadence** | Annual attestation | Semi-annual | Quarterly, with monthly metric review | Monthly, with continuous monitoring and defined alert thresholds |
| **Deployment route** | Standard pipeline | Standard pipeline with governance gate | Staged rollout with defined rollback criteria and a canary population | Staged rollout, formal go-live decision, documented back-out tested before launch |
| **Documentation set** | System record entry, named owner, tier rationale | Above, plus design decision record, delegation map, evaluation report | Above, plus data protection impact assessment, threat model, human oversight design, third-party assessment | Above, plus independent assurance report, resilience and exit plan, board paper |

**Decision rule for tiering: tier the system by what it can do without a human, not by what it is intended to do.** Intent is not a control. Capability is.

### Three worked classifications

**Case A. Contract clause extraction for the in-house legal team.** A retrieval-and-extraction assistant over the organization's own executed contracts. It produces a draft summary with citations. A lawyer reads it and issues nothing automatically.

| Dimension | Score | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Autonomy | 1 | Draft only, no state change |
| Reversibility | 1 | Bad draft is discarded |
| Stakes | 3 | A missed indemnity clause in a live negotiation is material |
| Affected population | 1 | Internal professionals who chose the tool |
| Data sensitivity | 4 | Privileged and commercially confidential material |
| External exposure | 1 | Internal corpus, no untrusted ingestion |
| Regulatory character | 1 | No specific regime identified for this use ⚠ |
| Novelty | 2 | Second deployment of an established retrieval pattern |
| **Total** | **14** | Band T2 |

Override 1 fires on data sensitivity at 4. **Final tier T3.** This is the classification most organizations get wrong: the system is low autonomy and reversible, so the instinct is to treat it as low risk, when data sensitivity carries the entire risk. The consequential control set is not oversight but confidentiality, retention configuration, retrieval permission filtering and privilege segregation, and T3 forces the data protection impact assessment and the third-party assessment that confidentiality risk actually requires.

**Case B. Claims triage for an external customer base.** Classifies inbound claims, routes them and can issue a "further information required" response directly to the claimant. Cannot decline a claim.

| Dimension | Score | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Autonomy | 3 | Issues customer-facing communications without review |
| Reversibility | 2 | A wrongly issued request can be corrected but was received |
| Stakes | 3 | Delay to a claim payment is a real consumer harm |
| Affected population | 4 | External individuals at scale, no practical opt-out |
| Data sensitivity | 3 | Personal data, potentially health-related |
| External exposure | 3 | Public-facing, ingests claimant-supplied documents |
| Regulatory character | 3 | Consumer and sector obligations likely attach ⚠ |
| Novelty | 3 | First customer-facing deployment for this organization |
| **Total** | **24** | Band T3 |

Override 1 fires on affected population at 4 and floors the tier at T3, which the computed band already reaches, so it changes nothing here. Record it anyway: an override that fires without moving the tier is what holds the tier in place if a later re-score drops the total, and a rationale that omits it will read as though the tier rested on the arithmetic. Override 2 is arguable, since routing affects the speed at which an entitlement is assessed but the system does not decide it; record the argument in the tier rationale rather than resolving it silently, and put the question to counsel ⚠. Override 3 does not fire, because reversibility is 2 rather than at or below 1, and override 4 does not fire, because novelty is 3 rather than 4. **Final tier T3**, with a documented re-tier trigger at the moment anyone proposes letting it decline a claim, which would move autonomy to 4 and stakes to 4 and land it in T4.

**Case C. Vendor onboarding agent.** An agent that reads supplier submissions, performs screening checks through tools, creates supplier master records and raises purchase orders below a threshold.

| Dimension | Score | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Autonomy | 4 | Multi-step agent, state-changing tools, runs to completion |
| Reversibility | 3 | A purchase order raised in error creates a contractual position |
| Stakes | 4 | Payment fraud, sanctions exposure, master data corruption |
| Affected population | 2 | Vendors and internal finance |
| Data sensitivity | 3 | Bank details, beneficial ownership, screening results |
| External exposure | 4 | Ingests documents from unvetted third parties |
| Regulatory character | 3 | Financial crime obligations attach ⚠ |
| Novelty | 4 | First agentic deployment with write access to a system of record |
| **Total** | **27** | Band T4 |

Override 3 does not fire, because it requires reversibility at or below 1. Override 1 fires four times over and override 4 is capped, the computed band already being T4. **Final tier T4.** The interesting output is not the tier but the design change it forces: at T4 an approval gate is required on irreversible steps, so the purchase order step must be separated from the screening step and gated, which is an architectural change decided at the same moment as the tier. That is governance by design working correctly. A tier that changes no design decision has not done anything.

### Tier drift, self-tiering and re-tiering triggers

**Tier drift** is the gap that opens between the tier a system was assessed at and the tier its current behavior warrants. It has four causes, and only the first is dishonest: scope creep, where capability is added without re-assessment; corpus creep, where the indexed material now includes a more sensitive class; usage creep, where a tool built for one team is adopted by another with different exposure; and dependency creep, where an upstream system the AI now calls has changed what it can do.

⧉ **Self-tiering by the requesting team is the largest single failure point in the tiering model.** The team scoring the system is the team whose delivery date depends on a low score, and no amount of guidance closes an incentive gap that direct. The three mitigations that work, in order of cost:

1. **Second-line calibration sampling.** Independently re-score a random sample of self-tiered systems each quarter, publish the disagreement rate and re-score the entire population of any team whose disagreement rate exceeds a threshold. This is the cheapest and it works because it makes optimism visible rather than punishing it directly.
2. **Objective triggers that bypass scoring entirely.** Any system with write access to a system of record, any system that ingests third-party content, any system with a public interface and any system touching special-category data enters at T3 minimum, regardless of the score the team produced. Take the judgment away where judgment is not needed.
3. **Separation of scorer from requester.** Effective and expensive. Reserve it for T3 and above.

Re-tiering triggers, as a fixed set of nine, each of which should be a monitored event rather than a policy sentence: a new tool added to an agent's allowlist; a change in the class of data the corpus contains; extension to a new user population or jurisdiction; a change in the model or model version by the provider; an incident of any severity; a material change in the regulatory character of the use ⚠; a change in the recorded purpose of the system or of its corpus; the departure of the named owner at T3 and above; and the lapse of the review cadence period.

### Tiering and risk-based regulatory schemes

Several regulatory schemes are themselves risk-tiered, classifying systems into bands with different obligations attaching to each. The architectural consequence, independent of any particular regime, is threefold:

- **Your internal tier is not a legal classification and must not be presented as one.** Keep them in separate fields on the system record. An internal tier quietly relabeled as a regulatory classification is a misrepresentation waiting to be found in discovery.
- **The classification input set is not the same.** Regulatory schemes tend to classify by use case and sector, meaning by what the system is for; internal tiering classifies by what the system can do. The two produce different answers for the same system and both are correct for their purpose.
- **The classification is an architectural input, not an output.** If a use falls in a band carrying specific obligations, those obligations constrain design before design begins, exactly as the entry-point and residency constraints do.

⚠ Which regime applies, which band a use falls into and what obligations attach are jurisdiction-specific determinations for counsel. Do not encode a regime's band names into the internal tiering scheme, because when the interpretation changes you re-plumb the control set rather than re-map one field.

What a regime demands of an architecture is smaller than its statutory text and more specific, and is organized here under four questions.

#### The four compliance questions

1. **What data may be processed, on what basis, for what purpose?** GDPR's lawful basis and purpose limitation; HIPAA's minimum necessary.
2. **Where may it be processed?** Residency, transfers and FedRAMP's authorized service offering constraint. This is where the entry point decision in 2.8 becomes a compliance decision.
3. **What must be retained, and what must be deletable?** The hard one in AI systems, because personal data ends up in chunks, embeddings, caches, logs and evaluation datasets. Keep the mapping from source record to every derived artifact, or you cannot execute a deletion request and cannot evidence that you did.
4. **Who is accountable, and can it be evidenced?** Audit controls, per-request attribution and a named human decision-maker where decisions affect individuals.

#### Three regimes in architectural terms

**GDPR.**

| Requirement | Architectural consequence |
| --- | --- |
| Lawful basis and purpose limitation | You need a basis and may not repurpose. Feeding a service corpus into a marketing model is a purpose problem before a technical one |
| Data minimization | Send and store only what the task requires. An argument for input redaction and for trimming what enters logs |
| Access and erasure rights | **Hard in a retrieval system**, for exactly the reason the third compliance question gives. The derived-artifact map, developed in 4.11, is what makes deletion executable and evidenced |
| Automated decision-making | Decisions made solely by automated means with significant effects attract specific obligations, pushing toward a meaningful human decision-maker rather than a rubber stamp |
| Transfers and residency | Where processing happens matters. The entry point and cloud platform decisions are where this is solved |
| Processor obligations | Model providers and infrastructure sit in a contractual chain |

**HIPAA.** Where the organization is a covered entity or a business associate, a business associate agreement is generally required with a vendor that creates, receives, maintains or transmits protected health information on its behalf, which gates model and platform selection ⚠. Minimum necessary. Audit controls, which bear directly on per-request attribution. De-identification as an architectural option.

**FedRAMP.** Federal use generally requires an authorized service offering, constraining deployment options before design begins ⚠. Boundary definition matters. Some controls can be inherited from an authorized platform, which is why platform choice is a compliance decision.

The cross-cutting consequences matter more than any single regime's detail: residency as a design constraint; retention and deletion designed in, including derived artifacts; logging that does not casually persist regulated content in readable form; tenant isolation enforced in retrieval rather than assumed; vendor and platform selection constrained by authorization and contractual status; and a named accountable human for any decision affecting a person's rights.

Two platform facts bear on this. **Prompt caching is documented as zero-data-retention eligible**, with key-value representations held in memory only and not stored at rest. And **cache entries are isolated between organizations** on every platform. Workspace-level isolation within an organization is the narrower and more easily misread claim: it applies on the Claude API, Claude Platform on AWS and Microsoft Foundry, while Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud are organization-level only. On those two platforms **workspace separation is not a data-separation control and must not be presented as one**. A design that relies on workspaces to hold two business units, two clients or two matters apart is therefore correct on some platforms and wrong on others, which makes the platform choice a confidentiality decision rather than a procurement one. Where tenant isolation is the concern, the retrieval filter is the thing you control; the cache isolation is a platform property. Both facts are developed at length in 2.7, which also maps these vendor brands onto the route menu in 2.8, and the isolation matrix sits in Appendix I with its verification date. **The three sites carry one claim and move together.**

The architectural consequence most often missed: **logs contain inputs and outputs, which means logs contain whatever regulated data the inputs contained.** Every observability decision is therefore simultaneously a compliance decision, including the monitoring design in 8.5. 4.8 turns that sentence into design.

#### AI-specific regimes in architectural terms

The three regimes above attach obligations to a class of data, to a sector or to a deployment environment. AI-specific law attaches them somewhere else: to a use, to a decision or to a role. That is why it cannot be absorbed by widening the privacy control set, and why it belongs in an architecture section rather than a compliance annex.

State the caveat once and do not repeat it. **Regime names, band boundaries, thresholds and commencement dates move**, and several of the regimes in scope for this reader are still acquiring the subordinate detail that will decide what they actually require. ⚠ Which regime applies, in which role, to which systems and what obligations follow are determinations for counsel in each jurisdiction. What does not move is the shape of the obligation. **The family shapes are what the architecture should be built against**, because a design built against a named statute has to be re-plumbed when the statute is amended, and a design built against the shape does not.

**Risk-tiered AI legislation.** The defining property is that **obligations attach to a classification of the use rather than to the technology**. The same model, retrieval pipeline and prompt asset sit in different obligation sets depending on what the system is for and who it affects. The corollary is uncomfortable for engineering: a system cannot infer its obligations from its components, and the component inventory that answers most other compliance questions answers none of these.

| Requirement | Architectural consequence |
| --- | --- |
| **Classification of the use** | The classification is recorded, dated, reasoned and defensible to a reader who starts from the opposite view. It is a field on the system record, held separately from the internal tier for the reason given above, and it carries the argument rather than only the conclusion. A classification that exists as a view held by the team that built the system is not an artifact |
| **Technical documentation** | Documentation becomes a **regulatory artifact rather than an internal one**: written for a reader outside the organization, versioned, retained and current at the moment of inspection rather than at the moment of build. The build consequence is that documentation acquires an owner and a generation trigger like any other evidence and stops being a phase at the end |
| **Post-market monitoring** | A continuing obligation, which means the architecture must emit evidence of operation across a period rather than evidence of design at a point. This is the operating-effectiveness distinction in 4.9 arriving as a legal requirement rather than as an audit preference |
| **Serious-incident reporting** | A clock. The obligation is not to report, it is to report inside a window that starts at an event the organization has to be capable of noticing. The incident process must detect, assess severity, reach a named decision-maker and produce a defensible position within the window ⚠ |
| **Human oversight** | Oversight must be **demonstrably capable of overriding**, not nominally present. An arrangement that cannot exhibit an override that changed an outcome is an arrangement nobody has tested. The five conditions in 4.6 are the design; override rate and override direction are the evidence |
| **General-purpose model obligations** | These sit upstream of the deployer and arrive as vendor documentation. The deployer's obligation is to **obtain it, retain it, version it against the model version actually in use and be able to produce it**, which makes it a procurement requirement fixed before signature rather than a request made after an inspection has started |

Two rows carry more design weight than their length suggests. **The clock is the row that breaks first.** Reporting windows in this family are short and start from awareness rather than from occurrence, which makes detection the load-bearing capability rather than drafting: an organization with a good incident template and a monitoring estate that surfaces a serious failure four weeks after it began will miss the window with an excellent report. Severity has to be assessable from the log without a reconstruction project, the escalation path has to reach a decision-maker outside working hours and the harm assessment has to run on partial information, because the window will not wait for certainty. The incident material in 4.12 and the incident row of the evidence register in 4.9 are where this is built.

**Upstream model obligations arrive as paper, and paper has to be caught at the contract.** A deployer that cannot produce the model documentation its own obligation depends on is exposed by an omission it did not commit, and the retention point is the one that gets missed: documentation obtained at onboarding and not re-obtained when the provider ships a new model version describes a system that is no longer running. Tie vendor documentation retention to the model version register, so a version change triggers the refresh. The documentation row's other consequence is not a longer document but a generated one, because a hand-maintained description of a system diverges from it within one release cycle and the divergence is the finding.

**Consequential-decision statutes.** The trigger in this family is neither the technology nor the sector. **It is a decision that affects a person's access to something they want**: employment, credit, housing, insurance, healthcare or education. Two properties matter architecturally. The system usually does not have to make the decision, because a system that screens, scores, ranks, prioritizes or filters ahead of a human decision is commonly within reach of the trigger ⚠, which places a large population of tools nobody describes as a decision system inside the family. And the trigger follows the affected person, so the applicable rules often follow where that person is rather than where the system runs, which is an entry point and residency question arriving from an unexpected direction.

| Obligation shape | Architectural consequence |
| --- | --- |
| **Notice** | Delivered at or before the decision. Timing is the constraint and it is a hard one: a statement published on a website is not a notice delivered at a decision. The decision path emits it, which means the decision path has to know that this decision is in scope, which means scope is a runtime property rather than a documentation property |
| **Explanation of the principal factors** | The system must be able to state why this decision, for this person, after the fact and possibly long after. Retrospective explanation is only possible if the inputs, the retrieved material, the model and prompt versions and the human steps for that specific decision were captured at the time. **This is a logging requirement wearing a transparency requirement's clothes**, and it is the row that most often turns out to be unbuildable a year later |
| **Human review or appeal** | A route to a human who can change the outcome. It is real when it has an intake, a service level, a competent reviewer, the authority to reverse and a record. It is advertised when it has a link. See the contestability property in 4.5 and the authority condition in 4.6. The cost is headcount, and it is the line most often absent from the business case |
| **Impact assessment on a cadence** | Periodic rather than a launch artifact, re-run on material change and retained. The architecture's contribution is to make the inputs to the next assessment fall out of operation, chiefly segmented performance, override statistics, complaint volume and outcome distribution, rather than be re-gathered by hand each cycle |
| **Record retention** | Long enough to answer a complaint that arrives late, which is longer than any operational retention an engineer would choose ⚠. The relevant clock commonly starts when the affected person learns of the decision rather than when it was made, so retention left at the log tier's default is retention set to the wrong number by accident |

The distinctive difficulty of this family is that it reaches decisions the organization was already making. Nothing in a screening step announces itself as regulated, the tool was often bought rather than built, and the population of systems in scope is discovered by asking what decisions the organization makes about people rather than by asking what AI it runs. That inventory question is a governance activity, not an engineering one.

One point deserves separating from the table, because it cannot be retrofitted. **An explanation produced after the fact is an artifact of what was recorded at the time, and nothing else.** A model asked to explain a decision months later will produce a fluent account that is a fresh generation rather than a record, which is a plausible narrative about a decision rather than an explanation of it, and the difference is the difference between evidence and a claim. If the retrieval set, the model version, the prompt version, the human intervention and the output for that decision were not captured, no later cleverness recovers them.

**Framework and basic-act legislation.** A national framework fixes duties, definitions, roles and institutional machinery, and leaves the operative detail to subordinate regulation, sector guidance and, in practice, to the first supervisory conversations. The architectural consequence is unusual: **the design has to be able to absorb a specification that does not exist yet.** That reads like an argument for waiting and it is the opposite, because two things are knowable well before the detail lands. The framework fixes who is in scope and in what role, and it fixes the duties in outline. What arrives later is the form each duty takes and the evidence that will be asked for.

| Fixed by the framework early | Arrives later | What the architecture builds now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Who is in scope and in what role | The tests that decide borderline cases ⚠ | The record of the facts that will decide the test: purpose, population, autonomy, data classes, jurisdictions |
| The duties in outline: safety, transparency, human oversight, documentation, redress | The specified form of each duty, often per sector | The duty discharged in the form good practice already requires, with the artifact named and owned |
| That sectors will get their own guidance | The guidance and its interaction with the sector regulator already supervising the firm ⚠ | A control register that maps many-to-many, so a new requirement lands on existing controls rather than creating a parallel set |
| That evidence will be required | The evidence format, the period and the retention | Continuous generation, because format can be rendered from a record and a missing period cannot be recovered |

**Obligations are met by artifacts that are already good practice, generated continuously rather than assembled on request.** An organization running tiering with recorded rationale, per-decision logging, a real oversight arrangement, periodic assessment and an incident process with a clock will find that most of what a subordinate regulation eventually specifies is a formatting exercise over records it already holds. An organization that waits will find the requirement arrives with an evidence period attached, and **a period cannot be retrofitted**, which is the most expensive discovery in this family and is made on a date somebody else chooses. The mirror failure is building to a draft: a control set engineered against a proposal that then changes leaves bespoke machinery, a sunk cost and no better answer than the generic artifacts would have given. Build the artifacts that every plausible version of the specification will want. Do not build the specification.

#### What the three families demand in common

Strip the three families of their vocabulary and the same five demands appear in each. This is what should survive when the names in it have changed.

| The demand | What it means in the architecture | Where it is built | Failure signature |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **A recorded classification** | The organization can state what this system is for, who it affects, what class it falls in and why, as of a date, with the reasoning attached | System record, tier record with rationale, architecture decision record | The classification exists only in a slide deck, or was written after go-live and reads like it |
| **An explanation of a specific decision after the fact** | For one named person and one dated decision, the system can produce what was retrieved, which model and prompt version ran, what the human did and what the output was | Audit logging in 4.8, retrieval provenance, prompt and model version pinning | The team offers to regenerate the answer, which is a new output rather than a record |
| **A human who can actually override** | A named, competent, resourced person who sees enough to judge, has time to judge, has the authority to stop it and whose objection has a defined effect | Human oversight design in 4.6, delegation map, appeals route | Approval rate at or near 100 percent and no case anyone can point to where an override changed an outcome |
| **Evidence of continuous operation rather than of design** | The control operated on every day of the period, and the population of events is demonstrably complete | Evidence register in 4.9, generation triggers, independent event count | Excellent design documentation and no operating record, which is the normal first-year outcome |
| **A clock on reporting** | The organization can detect a reportable event, assess it, decide and report inside a window that starts before anyone is certain | Incident process in 4.12, severity scale, pre-named commander, escalation that works out of hours | A good template, an unmeasured detection lag and a window discovered after it closed |

None of the five is exotic. Each is a control this document already requires for reasons that have nothing to do with AI-specific legislation, which is the argument for building them regardless of which regime lands. They also fail in a characteristic order. Classification is skipped first because it is paperwork before the interesting work. Explanation fails next and silently, because nothing goes wrong until somebody asks. Override degrades third, as volume rises and reviewer capacity does not. Continuous evidence is usually absent from the start and discovered in the first audit. The clock is discovered last and at the worst moment.

**The architect's job is not to know which regime applies.** That is a determination for counsel ⚠, it is jurisdiction-specific, and for any system built this year it will change at least once during the system's life. The architect's job is to build so that the answer to each of the five is yes before anyone asks. A system that answers yes five times is largely built for a regime nobody has finished writing. A system that answers no to any of them is exposed under all three families, and under whatever replaces them.

### ⌂ The architect's lens

**The enterprise question this section does not ask.** How does the system know at runtime which data is regulated, and which obligation currently reaches the backup and the evaluation set?

**Governance at this decision.**

| Decision here | Governance decision that belongs with it | Artifact and owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mapping source records to every derived artifact | A classification scheme whose labels propagate into chunks, embeddings, caches and logs | Classification standard, owned by information governance |
| Building for erasure | The preservation obligation that suspends deletion across the same artifacts | Legal hold procedure, owned by legal |
| Asking what must be retained | Retention applied per data class rather than per system | Records retention schedule, owned by the records function |
| Selecting a delivery route | Vendor due diligence, subprocessor chain and breach notification clauses | Third-party risk assessment, owned by vendor risk |

**What this costs the organization.** Several of these regimes carry hard notification deadlines, which turns detection latency into a regulatory obligation with a clock. The forgotten cost is the evaluation set: assembled early from production data, found late to hold personal data with no lawful basis, then rebuilt along with everything depending on it.

**The executive translation.** We can either evidence deletion, hold and residency across every copy of this data or we cannot, and that is designed in now or bought back later.

## 4.3 Model behavior controls: alignment, hallucination, consistency

Alignment asks whether the system does what was intended, why intention is hard to specify and how wide the instructing-to-guaranteeing gap is. It operates at two levels; confusing them is the error this section prevents.

**Model-level alignment** is the provider's work: training the model to be helpful, honest and to decline genuinely harmful requests. Real and valuable, and **not a control you can rely on for a consequential action in your system**: it shifts the distribution of behavior without constraining it.

**System-level alignment** is the architect's work: making the system do what was intended given a steerable but probabilistic model, the fourth of the four model properties in 2.2 turned into a design responsibility. **The line worth holding: alignment at the model level is Anthropic's problem; alignment at the system level is yours.**

#### What the provider's layer actually is, and why its shape matters to you

Model-level alignment is easier to reason about, and easier to describe to a regulator, once it is treated as an artifact rather than a disposition. Anthropic trains Claude against a **constitution**: a published written document describing the values and behavior the model should exhibit, revised over time. ⚠ The version in force is a perishable fact and the published version should be confirmed at the time any assurance statement relies on it; at the time of writing the most recent published revision dates from January 2026.

**The document is used in two ways during training**, and both are worth knowing because they explain the shape of what you inherit. It is used to generate the examples the model learns from, and to rank candidate responses. That is a mechanism for shifting a distribution, which is the same statement as "not a control you can rely on" made constructively rather than as a caution.

**It states a priority order for conflicts:** be broadly safe, be ethical, comply with the provider's guidelines, and be genuinely helpful to operators and users. Two properties of that ordering carry into design.

- **The ordering exists because helpfulness and safety genuinely conflict**, and a system that assumes they do not has no account of what the model will do when they do.
- **The ordering is holistic rather than strict.** Higher-priority goals generally take precedence, and the model weighs them together rather than applying a lexical sequence. **A holistic ordering is not a decision procedure, and it cannot be cited as one.** An assurance narrative claiming that a given category of output is impossible because safety ranks above helpfulness has over-read the document. What the ordering supports is a claim about tendency across a population of requests, which is the kind of claim an evaluation measures.

**The consequence for the boundary in this section is sharper than the general caution.** The provider's layer is general by construction, because it was fixed before your deployment existed. It has never seen the partner's domain policy, data-handling rules or authorization model. So a request can sit comfortably inside the model's general alignment and still violate a deployment-specific rule: disclosing another business unit's record, advising outside an approved script, releasing a figure the user is not entitled to. **The model cannot enforce a rule it was never given**, and the failure this produces is the quiet one, because the rule exists in nobody's layer and so nothing refuses, errors or logs.

⧉ **The most common way a safety design fails is not a control that breaks. It is a rule assumed into a layer that never held it.** The review question that catches it is mechanical: for each policy the deployment is bound by, name the layer that enforces it and the artifact that shows the enforcement. A policy whose answer is "the model handles that" has been identified as unenforced.

### The specification problem

Any rule simple enough to write down is too narrow, missing cases you meant to include or too broad, catching cases you did not. Hence explicit criteria beat dispositions, examples outperform rules for teaching judgment and over-refusal happens: a refusal rule tight enough to catch every genuine problem also catches legitimate work.

**The practical consequence:** every safety rule has a false-positive rate and a false-negative rate, and you choose where to sit rather than pretend you can have neither. Placing a control is that choice, the subject of 4.4.

### Reducing hallucination

Six documented techniques.

| Technique | Mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| **Allow Claude to say "I don't know"** | Explicit permission to admit uncertainty. Anthropic describes this simple technique as drastically reducing false information |
| **Use direct quotes for factual grounding** | For long documents, over roughly 20,000 tokens, ask for word-for-word quote extraction **first**, then perform the task on the quotes. Grounds the response in actual text |
| **Verify with citations** | Require claims to carry sources so they can be checked |
| **Best-of-N verification** | Run the same prompt several times and compare. Inconsistencies across outputs indicate hallucination |
| **Iterative refinement** | Use outputs as inputs to follow-up prompts asking for verification or expansion, catching inconsistencies |
| **External knowledge restriction** | Explicitly instruct Claude to use only the provided documents and not its general knowledge |

⧉ **No technique on this list eliminates fabrication.** Anthropic's caveat: these techniques significantly reduce hallucinations but do not eliminate them. A design assuming otherwise is wrong, and the remaining exposure is accepted in writing by the named business owner or it is not accepted at all.

### Increasing output consistency

Specify the exact format using JSON, XML or a template; **prefill the assistant turn** with the desired opening, bypassing preamble and enforcing structure; constrain with examples; ground answers in retrieval; break complex tasks into smaller consistent subtasks, each getting full attention. Structured outputs as a platform feature is the strongest version of the first.

### Risks and failure modes

| Failure mode | Detection | Control |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fabrication | Citation verification; sampled review | Citations; nullable fields; permission to say "I don't know"; quote-first grounding |
| **Over-refusal** | Refusal-rate monitoring; complaints | Narrow the refusal criteria; test with valid edge cases |
| **Direct injection / jailbreak** | Screen verdicts; repeat-offender patterns | Harmlessness screens; input validation; hardened system prompt |
| **Indirect injection** | Anomalous tool calls; output review | The eight-point checklist in 4.4 |
| Data leakage | Access-pattern review; deliberate probing | Permission filters before similarity; real identity to the backend |
| Sycophancy | Adversarial test cases | Instruct against it; independent review |
| Stale knowledge | Index freshness checks | Ingestion monitoring; require dates in output |
| Non-determinism | Repeat-run testing | Tighter criteria; structured outputs; schema validation |
| Context rot | Quality by conversation length | Compaction; context editing; note-taking; subagent isolation |
| Silent degradation | Drift detection; ongoing sampled review | Continuous evaluation, not just at launch |
| Cost blowout | Cost per outcome; cache hit ratio | Alerts; caching; context limits; retry caps |
| Over-automation | Design review | Human-in-the-loop on high-consequence paths |
| Attribution loss | Provenance audit | Structured claim-to-source mapping through every step |
| Compounding error | Error propagation review | Structured errors; local recovery; partial results with annotated gaps |
| Runaway loop | Turn counts; cost per task | Stopping conditions; maximum iterations |

Anthropic names the last two directly for agents: autonomy means higher costs and potential compounding errors, hence extensive testing in sandboxed environments with appropriate guardrails plus stopping conditions such as maximum iteration count.

**Failure is not emptiness**: a search that ran and found nothing is a successful answer; a search that could not run is a failure needing a retry decision. **What a failing component reports upward determines whether recovery is possible.** A structured report naming failure type, attempt, partial results and alternatives lets a coordinator retry differently, route around it or proceed with an annotated gap; "operation failed" forecloses that, and silent empty success is worse.

### ⌂ The architect's lens

**The enterprise question this section does not ask.** What happens to every system-level control when the provider ships a new model version, and who must revalidate before it reaches production?

**Governance at this decision.**

| Decision here | Governance decision that belongs with it | Artifact and owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Relying on system-level rather than model-level alignment | Recording the model, its version, its approved use and its revalidation date | Model inventory entry, owned by the model risk function |
| Taking the provider's refusal behavior as given | Mapping the provider's usage policy onto the enterprise acceptable use policy and resolving conflicts | Acceptable use mapping, owned by legal |
| Accepting that hallucination techniques reduce but do not eliminate fabrication | Written acceptance of the remaining exposure | Residual risk acceptance, owned by the business owner |
| Adopting best-of-N verification | Approving the cost multiplier on a production path | Cost model, owned by the product owner |

**What this costs the organization.** Model versions change on the vendor's schedule, so revalidation is a recurring operating line needing a maintained labeled test set. The forgotten cost is the version-pinning layer: nobody budgets it, everyone needs it the first time a deprecation notice arrives.

**The executive translation.** The model underneath changes on the vendor's timetable, so we fund revalidation as a standing cost rather than discover it as an incident.

## 4.4 Guardrails by layer and failure behavior

The safety question is concrete: what stops a working system refusing a valid request, producing an unfair outcome or taking an action no one approved? Over-refusal stands first deliberately: **a system declining valid work is a defect, not safe conservatism**, cutting against the instinct that more restriction is safer. The design skill is **placing each control and deciding what happens when one fails**, not naming them. Safety is a stack, not a feature; unfair outcomes belong to 4.5, this section to the stack.

### The layer model

Five layers: input, model, tool, output, process.

| Layer | Controls | Nature |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Input** | Request-shape validation; sensitive-data detection and redaction; **harmlessness screening**; scope check | Cheapest place to stop a problem |
| **Model** | System-prompt constraints; refusal conditions; the output contract; **structured outputs** constraining the response shape | **Probabilistic.** Necessary, insufficient alone |
| **Tool** | Only the tools the role needs; argument validation; preconditions; thresholds routing above-limit values to a human; approval gates for irreversible actions; rate limits; sandboxing | **Deterministic.** The strongest controls live here, because this is where actions happen |
| **Output** | Schema validation; policy checks; **citation verification** against retrieved sources; redaction; self-consistency checks such as recomputing a stated total | Catches what the model layer missed |
| **Process** | Audit trail; review routing; incident path; named owner; periodic review; **red-teaming** | Where accountability lives |

**The strongest controls live at the tool layer**: preconditions, thresholds, allowlists, argument validation and approval gates are deterministic, permitting an action or not; the model layer is probabilistic. **The governing rule:** where a rule protects money, identity, legal exposure or anything irreversible, the control is deterministic and sits outside the model.

A concrete input-layer control: **use a lightweight model such as Claude Haiku 4.5 to pre-screen input before the main conversation, with structured outputs constraining the verdict to a simple parseable classification.** Cheap, fast and deterministic to consume; the same pattern applies to tool output, point 7 below.

#### Choosing the check type at each point on the request path

The five layers say where controls live. This says what kind of check belongs at each of the three points where a decision is actually taken, and the answer differs by point rather than by preference.

| Decision point | A model-based check earns its place when | A deterministic check is better when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Input screening**, before the model call | Intent is ambiguous and you are catching jailbreak or injection patterns that cannot be enumerated. A lightweight classifier reads the input | The rule is crisp: a blocklist, a pattern match, a length or format check. Faster, predictable, and **it cannot be talked out of its decision** |
| **Output screening**, before the response reaches the user | You are judging a quality that needs language understanding: toxicity, tone, policy compliance. A judge model scores it | You are checking a known string, a forbidden field or a schema violation, where a validator answers with certainty |
| **Tool-call authorization**, before any side-effecting action | **Rarely, and treat any instance as a finding.** | **Almost always.** An allowlist of permitted actions, an identity check, a scope validation |

**The authorization row is the one that is not a trade-off.** Authorization must be **provable and replayable**: a reviewer has to be able to establish, after the fact, that this caller was permitted to take this action in this context, and to get the same answer running the check again on the same facts. A probabilistic authorizer cannot supply either property. That is a stronger statement than "deterministic is safer here"; it is that a model-based authorization decision is not evidence, whatever its accuracy.

**The two check types fail in opposite directions, which is the argument for chaining them rather than choosing between them.** A model-based classifier can be **evaded**, because an input can be phrased around it. A deterministic rule is **brittle**, because it blocks exactly what it was written to detect and nothing more, missing what nobody anticipated and over-blocking what merely resembles the pattern. No single control catches everything, so the design question is which control covers the other's named gap rather than which control is stronger.

⧉ **The three points check different things, so a control at one does nothing for the others.** This is the load-bearing sentence of the whole section, and the failure it prevents is concrete: a single output filter looks like a finished design on a diagram, fires where a reviewer can watch it work, and sits at the end of the path where the risk feels most present. It also runs after the only step on the path that could not be undone. A request arrives with no input screening, the model emits a tool call, the tool issues the refund, and the output filter then inspects the generated text and passes it, because the text describing a completed action is not unsafe text. **Output screening judges text. It does not judge actions.**

### The failure-behavior half

For every control, decide what happens when it cannot function. Three behaviors:

| Behavior | Use when | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Fail closed** (block) | Safety-critical, financial or irreversible actions | If the validator is unavailable, nothing goes out |
| **Fail open with alerting** | Blocking causes more harm than proceeding, **and** the action is reversible | A non-essential enrichment step is unavailable; proceed and flag |
| **Degrade to human review** | Capacity exists and the decision can wait | The classifier is uncertain; route to a person rather than guessing |

⧉ **A control with undefined failure behavior is not a control; it is an assumption.** A design adding a control without saying what happens on failure is weaker than one that does; a control that silently stopped working is a missing failure definition surfacing in production. Every fail-open choice is a held exposure, approved as one.

**Scope the failure-behavior question to the controls you operate, because the distinction matters in an audit conversation.** The three behaviors above govern **operator-built controls**: the screening services, validators, classifiers and authorization checks your team builds, hosts and configures. Those are the components that can time out, error under load or become unreachable, and therefore the components where a failure direction has to be chosen. **The provider's model-level safety behavior is not operator-configurable and presents you with no failure direction to choose**, because it is not a component you host, monitor or can watch degrade while your own traffic continues. How that layer behaves when it fails is the provider's property rather than an observable of yours, which is a reason to hold it outside the matrix and not a reason to assume it holds. Conflating the two produces two errors in opposite directions: a design that treats the provider's layer as a control it can tune, and a risk register carrying a fail-open exposure against a layer no control owner can configure, test or evidence.

**The failure mode this section is guarding against has a specific signature: a control that errors and still passes traffic looks healthy.** Requests keep flowing, latency may even improve, and the dashboards show a screening service that is being called. Nothing reports that it is returning nothing. That is why the choice has to be explicit: if it is not made, the surrounding code makes it, and the default in almost every framework is to let the request through. **An operator-built guardrail that silently passes traffic when it errors is worse than no guardrail**, because the design, the review and the register all record protection that is not present.

### Chain safeguards

The documented recommendation is to **combine strategies** rather than rely on one, with a multilayered example for a financial advisor chatbot: no single control suffices; the design question is coverage across layers, not strength at one.

### The removal principle

**Least privilege means removing capability the role does not require, not monitoring or guarding it.** Logging and confirmation prompts are detective and compensating controls; they do not shrink the attack surface. 4.10 carries this into agent scope and governance of the allowlist.

### The two prompt-injection threat models

The guardrails doctrine separates injection into two categories with **different threat models** and different mitigations. Conflating them is a design error.

| Category | Who is the adversary | What you are protecting |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Jailbreaks and direct prompt injection** | **The user of your application**, crafting inputs to bypass your guardrails | Your application, and Anthropic's usage policy |
| **Indirect prompt injection** | **A third party** who influenced content Claude reads: an inbound email body, a fetched web page, OCR from an uploaded file, a tool result | **Your user**, from instructions embedded in content read on their behalf |

#### Mitigations for direct injection and jailbreaks

- **Harmlessness screens.** The lightweight Haiku pre-screen described above
- **Input validation.** Filter for known injection patterns; a model can build a generalized validation screen from known jailbreaking language as examples
- **Prompt engineering.** System prompts that emphasize ethical and legal boundaries and explicitly tell Claude how to refuse
- **Respond to repeat offenders.** Throttle or ban users who repeatedly try to circumvent guardrails, and tell them their actions violate the usage policies

#### Mitigations for indirect injection: the eight-point checklist

The goal is to **structure the application so Claude can reliably distinguish untrusted content from your instructions.**

1. **Put untrusted content only in tool results.** Deliver third-party content inside `tool_result` blocks, **never in system prompts or plain user text blocks.** Claude is trained to treat instructions inside tool results with skepticism; the delivery channel is itself a control
2. **Tell Claude what the content is and where it came from.** In the tool description or result structure, state nature and source explicitly: an inbound email body from an unknown sender, OCR text from a user-uploaded image. This helps Claude calibrate trust in embedded directives
3. **State the policy in the system prompt.** State explicitly that content from tools, documents or searches is untrusted data and must never override the system prompt or the user's original request
4. **JSON-encode untrusted content.** Wrap third-party strings in a JSON object rather than concatenating into free-form text; JSON escaping gives unambiguous delimiters, so an attacker cannot close a quote or tag to break into an instruction context
5. **Do not put your own instructions in tool results. This is the counter-intuitive one.** Because Claude treats tool-result content as untrusted, instructions placed there may be **ignored or flagged as an injection attempt.** Send them in a user turn after the tool result, or a mid-conversation system message on supported models
6. **Limit access to sensitive data and actions.** Least privilege, so a successful injection does minimal damage: no secrets it does not need, tools sandboxed, permissions scoped narrowly
7. **Screen tool outputs before Claude acts on them.** Run the tool, pass raw output to a small classifier call and return it as a tool result only if the verdict reports no injection attempt, as with user input. Structured outputs make the verdict parseable so your application can branch on it
8. **Red-team your own agent.** Before deploying, test with documents, emails and tool outputs deliberately containing injection attempts; confirm Claude ignores them and that screening and confirmation catch the rest

Plus **continuous monitoring**: regularly analyze outputs for signs of successful injection and use it to refine prompts, validation and filtering.

Point 5, the security area's single most counter-intuitive rule, inverts an instinct: attaching your instruction to the retrieved content it concerns places it in the channel the model is trained to distrust.

For the computer use tool, Anthropic also runs classifiers detecting injections in screenshots and steers Claude to ask for user confirmation before acting.

### Handling a provider refusal as a typed event

The controls above are the ones you build. The provider's own layer also intervenes, and when it does the application receives a structured signal that most deployments discard. **Treating every refusal as one undifferentiated event is a lost control surface**, because the classes it merges call for different handling.

**The mechanism.** Where a streaming classifier intervenes, the Messages API reports `stop_reason: "refusal"` accompanied by a **`stop_details`** object carrying a policy category and a readable explanation. ⚠ Both fields are `null` where the refusal does not map to a named category, and the object itself is absent on models that predate the feature, so a handler must tolerate both and fall back to generic handling rather than assuming the shape. The category set is enumerated in the platform's stop-reasons documentation and is perishable: at the time of writing it includes `cyber`, `bio`, `frontier_llm` and `reasoning_extraction`. **Read the list at runtime or re-verify it at publish; do not hardcode it**, which is the same standing rule this primer applies to every platform enumeration.

**Why the category is worth routing on.** A refusal in one category is a user who has strayed near a boundary and needs a clear message. A refusal in another is a signal worth counting, attributing to a user or tenant, and feeding to the repeat-offender handling described above. A third may indicate the deployment is being probed. **These have different owners and different responses, and a single "the model refused" branch gives all of them the same one.** The refusal log is already an evidence artifact in 4.9, where the assertion it supports is that controls stopped things and that over-refusal is measurable; carrying the category into that record is what makes over-refusal measurable by class rather than in aggregate.

**The operational rule that is easy to miss: reset the conversation context after a refusal before continuing.** Remove or rephrase the turn that triggered it, or clear the history. Sending the next request on the same refused context tends to return further refusals, which presents to the user as a system that has stopped working and to the operations team as a cluster of unexplained failures. This is the refusal-handling equivalent of never retrying a 403: the condition is not transient, and repeating the request unchanged is not a strategy.

### ⌂ The architect's lens

**The enterprise question this section does not ask.** For each control in the five layers, who owns it, who tests it, on what cadence, and what evidence does the test leave behind?

**Governance at this decision.**

| Decision here | Governance decision that belongs with it | Artifact and owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Placing controls across input, model, tool, output and process | Assigning an owner, a test cadence and an evidence format to each | Control register, owned by the risk function |
| Choosing fail closed, fail open or degrade to human | Approving each fail-open choice as a held exposure | Failure behavior matrix, signed by the risk owner |
| Naming the layers in your own vocabulary | Mapping them onto the framework the auditor already uses, such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework | Control mapping, owned by compliance |
| Changing refusal criteria | Approval and test evidence before deployment | Change record, owned by the change advisory board |

**What this costs the organization.** Screening every inbound request is a permanent per-request charge plus an extra round trip growing with volume. The forgotten cost is evidencing: quarterly testing and evidence retention across the control set costs more than building it.

**The executive translation.** Every guardrail is a line item with a named owner and a test date, and the ones set to fail open are exposures we accept deliberately.

## 4.5 Fairness and transparency

Bias, fairness and transparency travel together although they are different obligations: the first two are properties of outcomes, the third a property of the relationship between the system and the people it affects.

### Differential treatment and differential outcome

Two distinct failures are both called bias, and conflating them is why fairness arguments in design reviews circle.

**Differential treatment** is the system doing something different because of a protected characteristic: a rule reading the attribute, an instruction directing different handling, a routing branch keyed to a group, a property of the mechanism usually visible in code or prompt. **Differential outcome** is measurably different results across groups by whatever route, a property of the output distribution invisible in the code by construction.

**An architecture can produce the second while containing none of the first.** No component reads a protected attribute, no instruction mentions one, every code path is identical, and outcomes still diverge: the corpus over-represents one population, a proxy carries the attribute's signal, one group's phrasing sits further from the training distribution and is understood less well, or a threshold calibrated on the aggregate falls elsewhere on each subpopulation's distribution. None of those is a rule about a group; all produce results about groups.

So **inspection of the design is not a fairness test**: a review establishing that no component reads a protected attribute has answered the easier question and reported it as the harder one. The only route to differential outcome is measurement, which requires knowing who is in which group. ⚠ Which of the two a non-discrimination regime reaches, and on what showing, is jurisdiction-specific and for counsel.

### Where bias enters a system you control

Five routes: the training data, which you do not control; **the retrieval corpus, which you do**; prompt framing that presupposes a conclusion; **proxy variables** correlating with protected characteristics; and feedback loops where outputs become the data for future behavior.

⧉ **The retrieval corpus is the bias source the architect most controls and most easily fixes, because the architect chose the corpus.** If the indexed material over-represents one region, client type or period, every answer inherits the skew. Training-data bias arrives with the model; corpus bias is a design decision and the route most often overlooked in review.

### Testing is segmentation

Measure accuracy and error rates separately by group, never in aggregate. The refinement: **equal overall accuracy with unequal error types across groups is still a fairness problem**, because a false positive and a false negative have different consequences for the person affected: a system erring toward denial for one group and approval for the other is not fair even when equally accurate for both.

The method is the same segmentation the evaluation material in 8.2 uses against deceptive aggregate accuracy: one technique, two purposes, quality problems there and fairness problems here.
