Whether an output attracts protection, who holds whatever rights arise, whether a license permits a particular machine use and what an indemnity covers are for counsel. What follows is the architectural position each has to land on and the artifact recording it.

### Output ownership and protectability

Two questions get conflated. **Ownership** is who holds whatever rights exist; **protectability** is whether any rights exist at all. Ownership as between organization and model provider is usually settled by the terms, which commonly assign whatever rights arise to the customer. Protectability is not settled by anyone's terms: no contract creates a right the law does not grant. In several jurisdictions protection depends on human authorship or a human contribution of a particular character, so a wholly machine-generated output may attract weaker protection than the organization assumes, or none ⚠.

The architectural consequence is a **recorded position, per output class, on whether the organization treats its AI-assisted outputs as protectable**, plus a **contribution record** where the answer matters: code that ships in a product, written material licensed to others, designs and brand assets. It does not matter for an internal summary and should be stated once per class rather than re-argued per artifact.

The contribution record is cheap while the work is happening and expensive afterwards, the shape of the purpose record in 4.13. It holds little: which prompt asset and model version produced the draft, which human edited it and what changed, most of which development tooling already emits. The failure is not difficulty but that nobody decides the record is needed until a dispute has made it retrospective, and a reconstructed contribution record is worth what a reconstructed audit log is worth.

The same question runs the other way: an output closely resembling a third party's protected work is an exposure rather than an asset.

### The provider's IP indemnity

Model providers commonly indemnify against third-party intellectual property claims arising from the customer's use of outputs. Read as a contract term it is commercial comfort; read correctly it is **an architectural constraint**, because its conditions are almost entirely statements about how the system is configured and operated.

| Typical condition | The architectural act that breaches it | Where that decision is actually made |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The model is used unmodified** | Fine-tuning, weight modification or distillation into a derived model | Model selection, usually early and usually on quality grounds |
| **Safety features remain enabled** | Disabling or routing around a provider-side protection, commonly to cut latency or reduce refusals | Guardrail design in 4.4 |
| **No knowing infringement** | Prompting for a named work, a named author's style or a competitor's material; ingesting material the organization knows it may not use | Prompt assets and the corpus |
| **Available mitigations are used** | Declining to enable a provider capability offered for this purpose, such as a citation, provenance or filtering feature | Platform configuration, often left at default |

**An indemnity conditioned on configuration is a constraint on the configuration.** The structural problem is a handoff: the contract is read once, by legal, at signature; the configuration changes continuously under engineers who have never seen it. Between them sits a protection any unflagged change can suspend, tested on the day it is needed rather than the day it lapsed.

The architect's job is narrow: **know which of the conditions the design has just breached, and say so at the design moment.** Not interpret the indemnity, which is for counsel ⚠, and not negotiate it. The control already exists in the evidence register in 4.9 as vendor commitment conformance, production configuration attested against contracted terms on a trigger. Extend it to the indemnity conditions: same attestation, same owner, more rows.

⚠ What a given indemnity covers, its cap, exclusions and procedural conditions are contract-specific and differ materially between providers. Notice conditions belong in the incident process, because an obligation to notify promptly is another clock.

### The right to index

This head gates most legal research, market-data, standards and analyst corpora, and it is the one the stakeholder table named. **A license permitting people at the organization to read a work does not automatically permit copying it into a vector store, generating derived representations of it or exposing its substance through an assistant** ⚠. Those are different acts from reading, performed by the organization rather than the named user who holds the seat, and subscription terms increasingly address them expressly, in both directions. The question is not whether the organization paid for the content, which it usually did, but what it bought.

The response is one field. **Every source in the knowledge source register carries a right-to-index value, populated before ingestion rather than after.** Four values are enough.

| Value | Meaning | Ingest decision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Permitted** | The terms expressly allow machine ingestion and derived representations for this purpose | Ingest |
| **Permitted with conditions** | Allowed subject to a restriction: attribution, no redistribution of substance, a named-user population, a retention or territorial limit | Ingest only if the condition is implemented as a control. A condition recorded as a note is not a condition |
| **Not permitted** | The terms do not allow it, or exclude it expressly | Do not ingest. Route the user to the source through a link or a tool call, so the work is consumed under the license that exists |
| **Unknown** | Nobody has read the terms against this question | **Do not ingest.** Unknown is a decision rather than the absence of one, and it is where most sources start |

⧉ **The right-to-index field is the cheapest control in this document and the one most often skipped.** It is one column, filled in by the person who already has to be asked to connect the source, at the moment of asking. Skipped, the identical question returns as reconstructing the provenance and license position of a live index while a counterparty's letter sits on the desk, its most expensive form. It also fails badly in discovery: the corpus is enumerable, the contracts are enumerable and the join between them is precisely the thing nobody did.

Two connections. The estate inventory in 5.1 has a sensitivity column answering whether content may be exposed to a population; right to index answers whether the copy may be made at all, so a source can pass the first and fail the second. **F11's knowledge source register carries the right-to-index column that records this**, populated before ingestion from the license or the contract and recorded as a basis rather than as a yes. Note whose signature it takes, because this is where the field is most often defeated: F11 separates the knowledge owner signing for authority, the data owner signing for access permission and the license holder signing for the right to index, and the third is routinely assumed to be covered by the second. Content arriving without a subscription, by scraping, by a pasted prompt or through a partner integration reaches the same index without passing procurement, a second reason to fill in F11's write-path owner.

### Open-source license exposure in generated code and dependencies

The exposure is real and ordinary: it attracts more anxiety than it deserves and less control than it needs. Two routes: generated code may reproduce material carrying license obligations, and an assistant that adds a dependency pulls in that dependency's license and transitive set.

Neither route is new and neither needs a new control. **The response is the same scanning and policy the organization already applies to human-written code, applied to a much higher volume**: license identification in the pipeline, an allowlist and denylist by license family, provenance for every dependency and a gate that blocks rather than warns. 7.5 already places license provenance in the secure development standard alongside static analysis, dependency scanning and secret scanning, the right home.

Volume changes two things and neither is the control. The gate must be automated and blocking, because a warning attached to code produced at this rate is a warning nobody reads. And the implicit check a human author performed while typing is gone, leaving the scanner as the only reader of the license question. The exposure that costs money is a copyleft obligation reaching a product the organization distributes, found in due diligence years later, when remediation is a rewrite on somebody else's timetable.

### The four heads and the artifact that answers each

| Head | The question it answers | Artifact that answers it | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Output ownership and protectability** | Do we own it, and is there anything to own | Recorded position per output class, plus a contribution record where it matters ⚠ | Legal, with the business owner |
| **Provider IP indemnity** | Is the indemnity intact given how this system is configured today | Vendor commitment conformance attestation, extended to the indemnity conditions | Vendor relationship owner |
| **Right to index** | May this source enter the index at all | Right-to-index field on the knowledge source register, populated before ingestion | Data owner, with counsel where the terms are unclear ⚠ |
| **Open-source license exposure** | What obligations arrived with the code | License scan output with a blocking gate, inside the secure development standard | Application security |

Three of the four are answered by a field or attestation that already has an owner, the fourth by a position stated once per output class; none is a program, and treating it as one is how it gets deferred.

### Trade secrets and the ingestion decision

One right behaves differently. **Trade-secret protection depends on maintaining secrecy and is lost through failure to maintain it** ⚠. The other rights survive a careless architecture; this one is extinguished by it.

**An ingestion decision that widens who can reach a secret through an assistant is a protection decision rather than a convenience decision**, and should be recorded as one, by name, when it is taken. Three cases recur: retrieval reaching an audience broader than the source system's access list, the permission-filtering failure in different clothes; material whose secrecy rested on the obscurity of a file share, which an index removes as a property of the material; and an output disclosing a secret's substance without citing its source, defeating every downstream handling obligation, because a recipient cannot protect what they do not know they hold.

The controls are the ones 4.13 specifies for privilege, applied to a different class of content: classify at ingestion, segregate the store, propagate the classification and mark the output. The corpus needing this treatment is usually small: formulations, pricing models, source code, customer lists, unpublished research and negotiation positions. Enumerating it is a morning's work, and the morning falls before the connector is configured, not after somebody notices how fluent the assistant has become on the subject.

## 4.15 Externally deployed systems

The worked examples here sit inside the organization; where one reaches an external population, as the claims triage case does, exposure is a tiering input rather than a design subject. Here it is the subject, because the reader will build one. **An externally deployed system changes the exposure profile rather than the architecture.** The controls are the same; their tolerances are not. Two shapes qualify and everything below applies to both: a system whose affected people sit outside the organization, and a system supplied into another organization's hands, which is the fourth of the role-moving acts in 4.7. The second shape carries one question the first does not, because the recipient becomes the deployer and the supplier sits upstream of them, and that allocation is a legal determination rather than an architectural one ⚠. What architecture owes it is the record described in 4.16 under binding legislation.

### What changes when the affected person is outside

| Property | Internal deployment | External deployment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The affected population** | Enumerable, reachable and bounded by the employee list | Unbounded and unknown. It cannot be surveyed, warned or retrained, and its composition, accessibility needs and languages are not known in advance |
| **The feedback loop** | An override, arriving in minutes from someone paid to look and competent to judge | A complaint, arriving in months from someone under no obligation to be accurate and with no view of what the system did |
| **The evidence** | Read by internal audit, which shares the vocabulary and starts from good faith | Read by a regulator, a claimant or a court, which shares neither and starts from the assumption that you would say this anyway |

The second row changes the design. An override is a signal about one output, from someone who saw what the system saw, in time to stop the consequence; a complaint is a signal about an outcome, months later, from someone who saw only the outcome, burden already assigned. **Everything the organization will want at that moment must have been captured at the time.** That is the audit logging in 4.8, with longer retention and a hostile reader.

### Disclosure and labeling

⚠ Whether disclosure is required, in what form and at what point, is regime-specific and a question for counsel. Treat it as a design decision regardless; it has two parts.

**Placement.** The cheap option is a line in a terms page nobody opens; the useful one is a statement where the person forms a belief about who they are dealing with, usually the first response rather than the first screen. A disclosure arriving after they have acted has disclosed nothing.

**Content.** Three things carry weight: that the response is machine-generated, what the system is and is not doing for them and how to reach a person. "AI-powered" answers none of the three; it is marketing, not disclosure. Record the wording and the reasoning: the disclosure is itself a representation ⚠ that will be read back alongside the interaction it accompanied.

### Capability claims

⧉ **The largest exposure in an externally deployed system is usually a sentence written by someone who has never seen the evaluation results.** A public statement about accuracy, coverage, expertise or reliability is a representation the organization must evidence, possibly years later, against a specific interaction, to an audience taking the least favorable reading ⚠. Neither side sees it: engineering because it is not in the system, the function that wrote it because the number came from a slide.

The control is procedural rather than technical. **No external capability claim is made until it has been reconciled against the evidence register**, recording claim, evidence, measurement conditions and owner together. Three tests, applied before the claim rather than after the challenge: is it measured or an adjective; what population was it measured on, and is that the population the reader will assume; would the same measurement give the same number today, on the current model version and corpus.

The recurring failure is a benchmark figure from a curated set restated as a general capability: true when measured, untrue of the reader's case, and that distance is what the organization must defend.

### Product liability and defect framing

Defect-based liability reaches software in more places than it used to ⚠, and its frame differs from every other in this part: not whether the organization was careful, but whether what was supplied was defective, measured against what a user was entitled to expect.

Three architectural consequences follow, all artifacts that exist before deployment or not at all.

- **A defined and documented intended use**, stated positively and narrowly, because expectation is measured against the use represented, not the use imagined by whoever finds it.
- **A stated set of known limitations**, specific enough to be actionable. A disclosed limitation forms part of what the user was entitled to expect; one known internally and undisclosed is the opposite.
- **A record of what the organization did about foreseeable misuse**, the one most often missing. Foreseeable misuse is a design input, not an operational discovery: red team findings, refused categories, guardrail decisions and why each was set where it was.

⚠ Whether any such regime reaches a given system, and what it would require, is a determination for counsel. Hold the three artifacts regardless: they are what an external system description needs and a procurement questionnaire asks for.

### Contestability

Contestability appears in 4.5 as what makes transparency usable; externally it is an obligation with a headcount. **The requirement is a route by which an affected person can reach a human who can change the outcome**, and the distinguishing word is resourced, not published: an intake that works for a non-user, a stated service level, a reviewer competent in the subject matter, authority to reverse and a record of the decision. A published address with no staffed queue is worse than no route: it converts a complaint into a documented failure to respond, better evidence for the complainant than for the organization.

### Retention

The complaint arrives long after the interaction, and the clock commonly starts when the person learns of the decision, not when it was made ⚠. **An evidence trail that has expired is indistinguishable from no evidence**, and the organization's position becomes whatever the complainant remembers. Two consequences: retention is set by the longest plausible complaint period rather than operational need, a number from counsel rather than the log tier's default; and the retained set must include what the person actually saw, the rendered output with its disclosures and interface context, not only the model's response, because the interface is part of the representation in dispute.

### The boundary this primer draws

**Most of this primer is written from internal deployments**, where the architect can enumerate the affected population, name the reviewers, reach every user with a change and see failures in the same week. Better stated than left implicit. It is not a different discipline: no external control set, only the controls above with a longer clock, a wider population and much lower tolerance for a claim the evidence cannot support.

## 4.16 Frameworks and control mapping

Frameworks are not interchangeable or competing answers to one question: they answer different questions and produce different artifacts. The practical failure is not choosing wrong but stacking several without a mapping, which leaves contradictory control definitions and a control population nobody can enumerate.

| Family | Primary use | Unit of analysis | Evidence produced | Limits |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Risk management frameworks** (for example the **NIST AI Risk Management Framework**, with its four functions to govern, map, measure and manage; **ISO/IEC 23894** as AI risk guidance; **ISO 31000** as the general risk parent) | Structure how risk is identified, assessed, treated and monitored | The risk, and the system it attaches to | Risk register, treatment decisions, residual risk acceptance | Voluntary and non-certifiable. Produces no independent assurance and no external certificate |
| **Management system standards** (for example **ISO/IEC 42001** for AI management systems, **ISO/IEC 27001** for information security, **ISO/IEC 27701** as a privacy extension) | Establish a repeatable management system with defined roles, objectives and continual improvement, capable of external certification | The organization and its management system | Certificate, statement of applicability, internal audit and management review records | Certifies that a system exists and operates. Does not certify that any particular AI system is safe or compliant |
| **Assurance and attestation standards** (for example **SOC 2** reporting against the **Trust Services Criteria**, and international attestation engagements in the **ISAE 3000** family) | Provide a third-party opinion to customers and counterparties | The service and its control set, over a period | A report with the auditor's opinion, control descriptions and test results | Scope is chosen by the reporting entity, so read the scope before the opinion. Design-only reports say nothing about operation |
| **Statutory and regulator expectations** (risk-tiered AI legislation ⚠, sector regulator guidance, supervisory model risk expectations for regulated firms ⚠) | Compel specific obligations by legal force | The use case, the sector or the regulated entity | Whatever the regime requires, plus regulatory correspondence | Jurisdiction-bound, subject to change and interpretation. Do not treat guidance as settled detail ⚠ |
| **Internal policy frameworks** | Bind the organization's own behavior and give the second line something to test against | The organization's own systems and staff | Policy, standards, exception register, attestations | Only as good as its enforcement. An unenforced internal standard is a documented gap |
| **Binding AI-specific legislation** (for example the **EU AI Act** ⚠, with its prohibited, high-risk, limited-risk and minimal-risk tiering, its separate obligations regime for general-purpose models, and its split of duties between provider and deployer) | Impose mandatory obligations that attach to a defined role in respect of a defined system, with penalties for non-compliance | The AI system and the role the organization holds in respect of it | Technical documentation, conformity assessment records, registration entries, instructions for use, post-market monitoring and incident reporting records | The determinations that matter most are legal ones: whether the system is in scope, which tier it falls into and which role the organization holds. Architecture supplies the facts; it does not decide any of the three ⚠ |

Five decision rules, one for each of the first five families:

- **Use a risk management framework when you need a common language for identifying and treating AI risk across teams that currently have none.**
- **Use a management system standard when a customer, regulator or board requires evidence that governance is systematic rather than heroic.**
- **Use an assurance standard when a counterparty needs independent comfort and will not accept your own attestation.**
- **Treat statutory and regulator expectations as design constraints applied before design, never as a compliance activity applied after ⚠.**
- **Use an internal policy framework to bind what no external framework covers, and keep it shorter than you think it needs to be.**

**Binding legislation is different in kind from the other five families and gets its own rule: identify the role before the control.** The others are entered voluntarily and scoped by the organization; a statutory regime is entered by operating a system, and its obligations follow the role the organization holds rather than how it describes itself, the determination 4.7 develops with the four architectural acts that move it. ⚠ Role, scope and tier are legal conclusions and must not be resolved from this document. Architecture owes them a record of fact precise enough to support them: what the system does, what it is used for, what data it processes, what a human can and cannot override and what changed since the last assessment. Most organizations cannot produce that record when asked.

⧉ **Stacking frameworks without a control mapping is the most expensive avoidable mistake in this area.** Adopt a risk framework, pursue a management system certification, commit to an assurance report and write your own standards, and without a mapping you run four overlapping control sets, four owners, four evidence collections and four internal audit cycles, meeting their contradictions at the worst moment.

### The control-mapping approach

**The control is the unit and the framework requirement is an attribute of it, not the other way around.** Five steps:

1. **Build one control register** with a stable identifier per control, its owner, its type (preventive, detective, corrective), its failure behavior and its evidence artifact. It is the organization's own list and does not change when a framework does.
2. **Map framework requirements onto controls**, many to many: one control commonly satisfies several requirements across several frameworks and one requirement commonly needs several controls.
3. **Collect evidence once per control**, not once per framework. The evidence register in 4.9 is organized this way deliberately.
4. **Identify contradictions explicitly** where two frameworks pull the control in different directions, most often on retention periods and on logging depth versus minimization. Three resolutions, in the order to try them: **split the artifact**, where the two demands turn out to attach to separable parts of it, which is the case worked below and is the only resolution that satisfies both; resolve to the stricter requirement, where one genuinely is stricter; or record a deliberate exception with an owner ⚠. **Reaching for the stricter requirement first is the common error**, because it presumes a ranking that frequently does not exist.
5. **Report by framework as a view over the register**, generated rather than maintained. Framework reporting maintained separately from the register diverges from it, and an auditor finds the divergence.

The same discipline applies downward to the layer names in 4.4: the organization's own control vocabulary maps onto the auditor's, and the mapping is an owned artifact rather than a conversation held once.

#### A worked crosswalk

The spine below is five controls from the evidence register in 4.9, given the stable identifiers step 1 requires. Columns are framework families rather than named standards, and each cell says what that family asks of that control rather than citing a clause, because clause numbers change and the asking does not.

| Control | Artifact it emits | Risk management framework asks | Management system standard asks | Assurance and attestation asks | Statutory and regulator expectations ask |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **C-01 Risk tiering** | Tier record with scores, overrides and rationale | Risk is characterized before it is treated, and the characterization is revisited | Scope covers this system, and risk criteria are documented and applied consistently | The control is described, the population of tiered systems is complete, and a sample shows the method was applied | Systems falling in a regulated class are identified as such before they operate ⚠ |
| **C-04 Human oversight operation** | Review event record: reviewer, decision, duration, changes | The chosen treatment is operating and residual risk is known | Competence for the role is defined and evidenced, and the procedure is followed | The control operated throughout the period, tested by sampling review events | A named human can reach a different outcome where a decision affects a person ⚠ |
| **C-07 Guardrail operation** | Control verdict log: which screens ran, verdicts, failure behavior invoked | Controls are monitored rather than assumed | Nonconformity is detected and corrected | The control operated per event, with completeness shown against an independent count | Processing was lawful and records are producible on request ⚠ |
| **C-11 Access entitlement** | Entitlement snapshot plus recertification record, human and non-human | Exposure from excess privilege is assessed and treated | Access is provisioned, reviewed and revoked under a defined procedure | Entitlements were reviewed at the stated cadence and exceptions were resolved | Access to regulated data is restricted and auditable ⚠ |
| **C-14 Vendor commitment conformance** | Production configuration attestation against contracted terms | Third-party dependency risk is identified and monitored | Externally provided processes are controlled | The subservice organization is carved out or included, and complementary controls are stated | Processor obligations and transfer conditions are met in fact rather than in the contract ⚠ |

Read it in both directions, each showing a different half of the relationship. Across a row, **one control satisfies four requirements from four different families and emits one artifact to do it.** C-04 is a single review event record answering the risk framework on whether the treatment operates, the management system standard on competence and procedure, the assurance standard on operation across a period and a statutory question about meaningful human involvement. Four requesters, one log. Without the mapping an organization produces that record four times, in four formats, on four cadences, owned by four people, and finds the discrepancies during an audit. Down a column, **one family's requirement is rarely satisfied by one control**: the assurance column's completeness demand reaches C-01, C-07 and C-11 together, because a population assertion about tiered systems differs from one about request-level verdicts and both must hold before any sampling means anything. Across a full register, **the number of distinct controls is far smaller than the number of requirements**, usually by a multiple.

The contradiction is where the exercise earns its cost. Take C-07: the assurance and statutory columns both want the control verdict log retained long enough to sample across a period and to answer a request arriving long after the event. The minimization requirement inside that same statutory family wants the opposite, because the log holds inputs and outputs and therefore whatever regulated data the inputs contained. Both are real obligations, and this is the case step 4 puts the split first for: neither requirement is stricter, so there is nothing to resolve to.

The resolution is architectural rather than legal, and the mechanism already exists: the split record from 4.8. **The contradiction dissolves once the artifact is separated into two artifacts with two retentions.** The governance skeleton carries the long retention that assurance and record-keeping need and holds no content; the content payload carries the short retention that minimization needs, behind a pointer. What goes on the register is therefore not "resolved to the stricter requirement" but a recorded decision naming both requirements, the split, the two periods and the owner. ⚠ The periods themselves come from counsel rather than from this table. The general shape: **contradictions between frameworks live at the edges, where two regimes want opposite things from the same artifact**, and they are almost never resolved by picking a winner but by discovering that the artifact was a single thing only because nobody had had a reason to split it.

#### Reading and holding a certification

A General Counsel reads other parties' certificates far more often than pursues one, and reading one has a fixed order of operations.

**A certificate is a statement about a management system, not about a system.** It records that an accredited body examined how the organization sets objectives, assigns roles, assesses risk, operates controls, audits itself and corrects what it finds, and concluded the machinery is present and running. It says nothing about the quality of any output, the safety of any deployment or the lawfulness of any use: an organization can hold a certificate and run a system that should never have been built, provided the decision to build it passed through the machinery.

**The first question of any certificate is its scope.** Scope is a sentence on the certificate naming the activities, locations and services covered: the whole organization, or one product line, in one country, at one site. A narrow scope is the most common way a certificate conceals what its reader assumes it covers, and the concealment requires nobody to lie: the scope statement is on its face and the reader skipped it, having looked only for the logo. A vendor whose certificate covers corporate infrastructure and not the service you are buying has told you so, in one line, on the document you accepted.

**The statement of applicability is the artifact to ask for, rather than the certificate.** It lists which controls were applicable and which were excluded, with the reasons. The exclusions are the information. A certificate tells you that a system was audited; the statement of applicability tells you what it was audited about. Read the exclusions first and treat a refusal to share it as an answer, since it is routinely shared under a confidentiality undertaking in ordinary diligence.

Certification runs in **two stages**: a documentation review, then an audit of operation evidenced by records generated in the ordinary course of running the organization. **Stage two is the stage that fails**, for the same reason first assurance engagements fail in 4.9, and it is not an event: **surveillance audits** follow, typically annual and sampling part of the system, with a full **recertification** closing a multi-year cycle. A certificate therefore says the system was operating at the last visit and was adequate at the points sampled, so one produced eleven months into the cycle has eleven months of unexamined operation behind it, and an unsampled area has not been examined. The audit reports are worth more than the certificate to anyone doing real diligence.

Findings come in two grades. A **minor nonconformity** is a lapse inside an otherwise functioning process, such as a record not kept or a review held late, attracting a corrective action with a due date while the certificate stands. A **major nonconformity** is a failure of the process itself, or a lapse severe enough to break the assurance, and it suspends or blocks the certificate until the correction is verified. For a live system: a minor against a control your system depends on means the control operates and slipped, so the question is whether it slipped on your system during the period; a major means the control cannot be relied on for that period, so every assertion resting on it is unsupported until re-verified, including assertions already made to your own board or to a client.

The practical rule for reading a counterparty's certificate, in order: **scope first, statement of applicability second, date and surveillance status third and the certificate itself last.** By then you know what the certificate is worth, and in most vendor conversations the first three questions establish whether anyone on the other side has read it either.

⚠ Be careful with framework names, versions and content in any document that leaves the building: misdescribing what a standard requires is a credibility failure with the specialist audience who reads these documents. Where you are not certain of a standard's content, state the control you operate and the assertion it supports, and let someone who has read the current text confirm the mapping.

## 4.17 Operational resilience

### Dependency mapping and the model provider as a critical third party

Resilience begins with what the system depends on, and AI adds dependency classes traditional mapping misses. Eight dependency classes: the model provider and specific model version; the inference platform or cloud region; the retrieval store and its index; the embedding model, a second, separately versioned model dependency; the source systems behind the corpus; the tool endpoints the agent calls; the identity provider; and human reviewer capacity, a dependency in the strict sense: the system cannot run at rated throughput without it.

The model provider is a **critical third party** in the operational resilience sense: a supplier whose failure would prevent delivery of an important business service. Contractually it attracts the assessment, monitoring, exit and, in regulated sectors, notification treatment given to critical suppliers ⚠. Architecturally the substitution question must be answered before it is asked in anger.

### Concentration and substitutability

Concentration risk in AI is understated because it is counted at the wrong level. Three AI products are one dependency if all three share provider, region and model family. Count concentration at the level of the shared failure, not the number of systems.

Substitutability is the honest measure of exit capability, in four levels.

| Level | Meaning | Typical time to switch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **L0 Locked** | Provider-specific features are load-bearing; prompts and evaluation are tuned to one model; no abstraction | Rebuild |
| **L1 Portable with rework** | Abstraction exists but prompts and evaluations are model-specific | Months |
| **L2 Substitutable** | Abstraction plus a maintained evaluation suite that runs against any candidate model | Weeks |
| **L3 Dual-run** | A second provider is configured and periodically exercised with live traffic | Days or less |

**Decision rule for substitutability: set the target level by tier, not by preference, and note that the evaluation suite is the thing that makes substitution possible.** Without one you cannot know whether the substitute is acceptable, so exit planning that does not fund evaluation is a document, not a capability.

### Degraded modes and the manual fallback

Every AI-dependent process needs a defined answer to what happens when the AI is unavailable, wrong or too slow, and it must be a mode, not an aspiration. Four modes, in descending order of capability:

1. **Full service.** Everything operating.
2. **Reduced capability.** A smaller or older model, narrower tool set, longer latency, higher human review rate. Defined thresholds trigger it automatically.
3. **Human-only.** Runs as the process did before the system existed, at reduced throughput; requires a manual path that still exists, people still trained on it and honest capacity assumptions.
4. **Suspended.** Stops, with defined communication to affected parties and a defined authority to declare it.

⧉ **The manual fallback is the control that quietly disappears.** Present at launch, it decays over the following year as staff who knew the manual process leave and headcount is cut on the strength of the automation, and is found non-functional when needed. The remedy is to exercise it on a schedule with real volume, not document it. An untested fallback is an assumption, exactly as an untested control is.

### Recovery objectives and testing

Conventional recovery time and recovery point objectives apply and are insufficient. AI systems need a third, with no standard name, defined locally: **the recovery quality objective**, the minimum acceptable output quality during degraded operation, expressed against the evaluation suite. Without it, a system technically available while producing materially worse outputs is reported as recovered.

Resilience is tested, not documented, and the AI test set has six scenarios, in ascending order of neglect: provider outage; region failure; retrieval store unavailable, interesting because the system may keep answering from parametric knowledge, confidently wrong rather than obviously broken; tool endpoint failure; reviewer capacity shortfall; and the sixth.

### The scenario nobody plans for

**The model provider changes the model under you.** Not an outage: nothing fails, latency is normal, errors are absent and outputs differ in ways that may be better on average and worse on the cases that matter. It is the single most likely materially disruptive event in an AI system's life and the least represented in continuity plans, which are organized around unavailability.

Five architectural requirements follow, each cheap at design time:

1. **Pin the version explicitly.** Never depend on a floating alias in production above T1.
2. **Log the model identifier and version on every request**: the first question when quality changes is which model produced this.
3. **Maintain a continuously running evaluation suite** so behavior change is detected by measurement rather than complaint.
4. **Track deprecation notices as a governance event with an owner**, not an engineering ticket: a forced version change is a re-tier trigger and a change-control event.
5. **Treat a provider-initiated model change as a change requiring pre-change and post-change evaluation evidence**, exactly as an internally initiated change would be. Not choosing it does not alter your accountability.

## 4.18 Governance in the architecture, section by section

This part in operational form is a row per architectural decision: the decision, the governance decision that must be made at the same moment, the artifact that decision leaves and the person accountable for it. None of those rows is new here. Each sits in the section where the decision is actually made, inside that section's **⌂ The architect's lens** block, in its own "Governance at this decision" table. In the order the rows run, they are carried by the lens blocks in 2.4 for pattern selection, 1.3 for delegation, 5.3 for retrieval design, 2.6 for model selection, 2.7 for prompt assets, 3.2 for tool design, 2.8 for entry point and delivery route, 3.7 for the gateway control point, 2.13 for memory and state, 8.2 for evaluation and 8.1 for deployment.

Four of those decisions run on into a second section that carries no lens block of its own: 5.4 develops retrieval as a system, 2.11 the model portfolio, 1.7 reusable workflow assets and 2.15 production deployment. The governance row for each stays with the partner section named above, so a reader who turns to the second section will not find a second one there. **This is deliberate. The row belongs where the decision is taken, not wherever the topic is discussed**, and duplicating it would create two owners for one artifact, which is the failure 4.7 exists to prevent.

The test is the same for every one of them. If a row can be answered for a live system with a team name rather than a person, or with a practice rather than an artifact, that row is a finding.

The argument of this part is what the rows show together rather than what any one of them says: there is no row where the governance decision could sensibly be made later, and there is no row where making it later would be cheaper.

## Governance by Design: the one-page version

1. **Thesis.** Governance that arrives after the architecture is a review, not a control. Every architectural decision has a governance consequence, decided at the same moment, by a named person, leaving an artifact.
2. **Operating model.** Three lines of defense, breaking for AI on competence inversion, speed asymmetry, vendor opacity and a diffuse first line. A committee that can say no on a Tuesday. Policy, standard, procedure and control kept distinct. Placement follows authority; competence is purchased.
3. **Tiering.** Eight inputs scored 0 to 4, four overrides that restore the asymmetry additive scoring destroys, four tiers and seven things that change per tier. Tier by capability, not intent. Self-tiering is the weak point; calibration sampling and objective triggers are the fix. Internal tier is not a legal classification ⚠. Four compliance questions: what may be processed and on what basis, where, what must be retained and deletable and who is accountable.
4. **Model behavior.** Model-level alignment is the provider's; system-level alignment is yours, and the model's training is not a safety control. Every rule has a false-positive and a false-negative rate. Six hallucination techniques that reduce and do not eliminate fabrication, five consistency techniques, fifteen failure modes with detection and control.
5. **Guardrails.** Five layers, with the strongest controls at the tool layer because that is where actions happen. Three decision points, and they check different things, so a control at one does nothing for the others. Where a rule protects money, identity, legal exposure or anything irreversible, the control is deterministic and sits outside the model. Three failure behaviors, and a control with none is an assumption. Over-refusal is a defect, and a provider refusal is a typed event to be routed on its category, counted and followed by a context reset rather than discarded. Remove excess capability rather than logging it. Two injection threat models and the eight-point checklist.
6. **Fairness.** Differential treatment is a property of the mechanism, differential outcome a property of the distribution, and an architecture can produce the second containing none of the first. Five routes for bias, and the corpus is the one the architect chose. Segmentation is the test, and equal accuracy with unequal error types is still unfair, but the fairness criteria cannot all hold at once, so the criterion is selected and recorded before the measurement ⚠. Generative systems have no score to threshold, so evaluate at the decision rather than the text. Group labels come from collected attributes, inferred proxies or counterfactual probes, at different evidential worth. The bias test plan fixes the question before the answer is known. Remediation by group is a legal decision ⚠. Four transparency commitments, plus contestability and accountability.
7. **Oversight.** Five requirements: information, time, competence, authority, incentive. Six failure modes. Six measurement instruments. A 100 percent approval rate is evidence of failure.
8. **Ownership.** One named person per asset, with a deputy who has done the job. Decision rights fixed across eight lifecycle stages. Go-live authority moves with tier; design and data accountability do not. Vendor owns the weights; you own everything else, including the assertion that the running configuration matches the contract. The prior question is which regulatory role the organization occupies, which turns on four architectural acts and belongs on the decision record ⚠.
9. **Logging.** Fifteen fields, including what did not happen. Immutable, integrity-verified, time-synchronized, retained to a legal driver, with access to the log itself controlled and logged. Split the record to reconcile accountability with minimization.
10. **Evidence.** If a control cannot produce evidence on demand it is a claim. Design-time evidence and operating-effectiveness evidence are different assertions and auditors test the second. Completeness sinks first audits: build the independent count on day one.
11. **Access.** Identity, authentication, authorization and entitlement. Agent scope is the intersection of user, task and role. Filters before similarity, with negative probe tests. Segregation of duties collapse is the under-detected failure. Joiner, mover, leaver for non-human identities, reviewing scope rather than existence.
12. **Privacy.** Seven principles restated as obligations. Minimization against the context window, purpose limitation against reuse, lawful basis as an input ⚠. Six rights as engineering requirements. Erasure reaches six derived stores and requires a map built before the first request. No training use and bounded retention are two claims and are routinely collapsed into one ⚠.
13. **Security.** STRIDE adapted plus eight AI-specific threats. Three trust boundaries with four rules. Secure defaults. Red teaming on change with a calendar floor. Packaged capability enters on an audit against its stated purpose, runtime confinement and a trusted-source policy, with a recorded verdict, because the bundle arrives before any request does. AI incidents have no stack trace, do not reproduce and may harm reputationally or legally. Nobody owns the corpus write path.
14. **Privilege.** Confidentiality and privilege are different obligations and the second fails catastrophically ⚠. Six design choices that improve the factual position. Classify at ingestion, segregate the store, propagate the tag, mark the output. The log is the largest exposure. Legal hold must be buildable before it is needed.
15. **Intellectual property.** Four heads: output ownership and protectability, the provider indemnity and the configuration choices that suspend it, the right to index and open-source exposure in generated code. A reading license is not an index right, and the right-to-index field on every source is the cheapest control in this part and the one most often skipped. Widening who can reach a secret through an assistant is a trade-secret decision ⚠.
16. **Externally deployed systems.** Same controls, longer clock, wider population, lower tolerance. Disclosure is a design decision about placement and wording. A capability claim is a representation the evidence register has to support before it is made. Intended use, stated limitations and a record of what was done about foreseeable misuse are the defect-framing artifacts ⚠. Contestability must be resourced rather than published, and retention has to outlast the complaint.
17. **Frameworks.** Six families, six uses, six artifacts, six limits. Binding legislation is different in kind from the other five, so identify the role before the control: obligations follow the role the organization holds rather than the way it describes itself ⚠. One control register, many-to-many mapping, evidence collected once, contradictions surfaced at the edges and resolved by splitting the artifact, reporting generated. A certificate is a statement about a management system, so read scope first and the statement of applicability second.
18. **Resilience.** Eight dependency classes. Concentration counted at the shared failure. Four substitutability levels, made possible by the evaluation suite. Four degraded modes and a manual fallback that decays unless exercised. A recovery quality objective alongside time and point objectives. The provider changes the model under you.
19. **The closing test.** For any live system, take any architectural decision and ask for the governance decision, the artifact and the person. A team name is a finding. A practice with no artifact is a finding. A decision made later than the architecture is the finding this part exists to prevent.
